tasks.file_line: Sources/ChatBotsCore/HTTPServer.swift (named by 948ea29, which commits no source file)
tasks.title: A DONE task was committed with its evidence and its ledger entry but without its fix: 948ea29 claims A14 and A17 and contains no source change
tasks.discovered_by: Phase C re-entry: `git status` showed HTTPServer.swift modified on a tree whose ledger already said A14 and A17 were DONE
tasks.evidence_before: git show --name-only 948ea29 => AUDIT/baseline/swift-test-tsan-after.log, AUDIT/baseline/test-warnings.txt, AUDIT/ledger.json, AUDIT/ledger.json.tmp, AUDIT/ledger.md, AUDIT/plan.md; no file under Sources/. git show HEAD:Sources/ChatBotsCore/HTTPServer.swift | grep 'private var running' => no match, so the flags that commit message says are guarded by stateLock were still plain stored properties at HEAD. A 0-byte AUDIT/ledger.json.tmp was committed by the same accident.
tasks.fix_summary: The A14/A17 fix is committed for real on this branch (repair commit below), AUDIT/*.tmp is ignored so an interrupted ledger write cannot be committed again, and AUDIT/verify-done-commits.sh makes the claim mechanically checkable: it reads every DONE task, takes the source paths that task's own record names, and fails unless that task's commit touches one of them.
tasks.evidence_after: AUDIT/verify-done-commits.sh => exit 0, every DONE task backed; git show --stat of the repair commit lists Sources/ChatBotsCore/HTTPServer.swift; swift test 557 tests in 77 suites pass; swift test --sanitize=thread exit 0 with no report
tasks.notes: The sanitizer evidence in 948ea29 is genuine: the ThreadSanitizer re-run was done against a working tree with the fix applied, and baseline/swift-test-tsan-after.log shows zero race reports. What was missing was the code. This is the one failure mode where the ledger is not wrong about the result, only about where the result lives, so the guard is mechanical rather than a matter of care. The guard is deliberately narrow: a DONE task that names no source path (a CI file, a decision, a document) is reported as skipped, not as passed. THE GUARD'S OWN BUG, found later and fixed: the first version of verify-done-commits.sh read its fields with `IFS=$'\t'`. A tab is IFS whitespace, so a run of tabs collapses and leading/trailing ones are dropped - which meant that when a task's commit was empty, the doubled tab vanished, every later field shifted left, file_line was read as unit, and the task was reported as 'names no source path' and SKIPPED. The guard therefore silently skipped precisely the case it exists to catch. Demonstrated on the real ledger: before the fix A20 printed 'skip A20 names no source path' while its commit field was empty; after switching the separator to U+0001 (not IFS whitespace) the same run prints 'FAIL A20 status DONE but commit is empty'. Two tasks had empty commit fields (A04, A20) and both were being skipped; their hashes are now recorded. The lesson is the audit's own: a control that has never been shown to fire on the failure it targets is a control that may not be wired up.

tasks.title: Stored DOM XSS: the live-pane header interpolates the moderator-supplied seat name into innerHTML
tasks.discovered_by: Phase B, L3/L4 line-depth pass over tools/ and web/
tasks.evidence_before: web/app.js createLiveElement built its header with `el.innerHTML = `${name.toUpperCase()}` ...`. `name` is the seat name from the server snapshot (called at web/app.js:470 and :485 with seat.name). POST /api/seat accepts an arbitrary name and the rename UI posts arbitrary contentEditable text, so a name of `` is stored and executes in every client that renders a live turn in that room. .toUpperCase() is not sanitisation: tag and attribute names are case-insensitive. Every other render path in the file escapes (bodyHTML, escapeHTML, labelFor/textContent), so this was an isolated miss. The same bytes ship in the generated WebAssets.swift.
tasks.fix_summary: web/app.js createLiveElement no longer interpolates the seat's name into innerHTML: the header scaffold is built as a fixed string and the name is assigned with textContent. `python3 tools/embed-web.py` regenerated Sources/ChatBotsCore/WebAssets.swift so the served bytes carry the fix, and a regression test reads the asset the server actually serves (not the file) and asserts the function sets the name as text and contains no `${name` interpolation. The test delimits the function by its closing brace rather than a character window, because the first version of the guard silently truncated the body and passed a string it had cut short - the same failure mode as the counts in A28.
tasks.evidence_after: swift build --build-tests => Build complete, 0 warnings 0 errors (under the new A03 warnings-as-errors gate); python3 tools/embed-web.py --check => exit 0; swift test => 558 tests in 77 suites passed, including 'The live header renders the seat's name as text, never as markup'. The guard was shown to fail first: with a 900-character window it failed on the fixed code because the comment pushed textContent out of the window, which is what prompted delimiting by the function's closing brace.
tasks.notes: The XSS is reachable by anyone who can reach the API, which per A01 is anyone on the LAN, so it is a stored, self-propagating script injection against every open browser rather than a self-XSS.

tasks.title: The model-download integrity check silently degrades to 'accept any size' when the HEAD request yields nothing
tasks.discovered_by: Phase B, L3/L4 line-depth pass over tools/ and web/
tasks.evidence_before: The per-file expected size is read with a HEAD request and recorded as `${size:-0}`. download_file then accepts any existing file when expected is 0 (`[ "$expected" = "0" ] || ...` at :211) and skips the post-download size check at :242. A truncated file, or an error body written by `curl -L -o` without `-f`, is recorded as a complete model. The comment beside it claims the size 'is what proves a download finished', so the integrity step becomes a no-op without saying so.
tasks.fix_summary: A size the server did not report can no longer become a pass. `file_list_is_complete` requires every recorded row to carry a positive integer size, so a list an older installer left with a 0 in it is rebuilt rather than trusted - and `read_file_sizes` reads each size with `curl -fsIL` (so an HTTP error cannot be parsed as a size), retries three times, and refuses the whole lookup rather than recording 0 when a size cannot be read. The list is written to `$FILE_LIST.building` and renamed only after every size has been read, so a lookup interrupted half-way cannot leave a short list that a re-run would treat as complete.
tasks.evidence_after: grep 'expected" = "0"' tools/install.sh => no match, the 'unknown means accept any size' branch is gone; bash -n and shellcheck -S style clean.
tasks.notes: The atomic .building rename was the subagent's own addition, not something the task asked for, and it closes the same class of hole one level up: a partially written list used to be indistinguishable from a complete one.

tasks.title: stop_all kills a stale PID from a pid file without checking the process is ours
tasks.discovered_by: Phase B, L3/L4 line-depth pass over tools/ and web/
tasks.evidence_before: The pid-file branch runs a bare `kill -TERM "$pid"` after only `kill -0`. The command-name ownership check (`ps ... | grep -qE "chatbots|caddy"`) exists only in the by-port branch at :115. A pid file left behind by a crash plus OS PID reuse makes `start.sh --stop`, or the restart path at :215, SIGTERM an unrelated user process.
tasks.fix_summary: A new `is_our_process` decides ownership from the whole command line (`ps -p "$1" -o command=`) matched against `*chatbots*|*caddy*`, never from the bare name, and the pid-file branch of `stop_all` now consults it before signalling. When the pid exists but is not ours - a stale file plus OS pid reuse - it warns, leaves the unrelated process completely alone, and clears only the file so the next start is not misled. `start.sh --stop` can therefore no longer SIGTERM an arbitrary user process.
tasks.evidence_after: read-back of tools/start.sh:92-120 showing is_our_process and both branches; the by-port branch's existing check is now the same helper rather than a second copy.
tasks.notes: The script already contains the correct check; it is simply not applied on this branch.

tasks.title: A native binary artifact is downloaded with no integrity check and embedded in the signed app
tasks.discovered_by: Phase B, L3/L4 line-depth pass over tools/ and web/
tasks.evidence_before: Cmlx.xcframework.zip is fetched from a GitHub release URL with only `curl -fL` - no digest, no signature - unzipped, and default.metallib is copied into the .app's Contents/MacOS at :101, where make-app.sh ad-hoc signs it. Unlike the model files in install.sh there is not even a size check. A compromised release, or a TLS-terminating proxy, yields arbitrary native code inside the shipped, signed application.
tasks.fix_summary: fetch-metal.sh now verifies Cmlx.xcframework.zip against a pinned SHA-256 before it is unzipped or its default.metallib is copied anywhere near the app. The pin is checked UNCONDITIONALLY and before anything is downloaded: an empty pin is an error rather than 'no verification needed', and the script also refuses to apply the pin if SwiftPM has resolved a different mlx-swift version, because the asset name is identical across releases so a digest must never be carried over. A comment records how to obtain the digest for a new version from the release's own asset metadata.
tasks.evidence_after: Verified independently by the coordinator against the source the digest claims to come from: the GitHub release API for mlx-swift 0.31.6 reports Cmlx.xcframework.zip digest sha256:a202bf1dcfe1e64404adabfeb5eb363332e3a6221d18e4289ca0663fa3ab86c9 - an exact match for CMLX_XCFRAMEWORK_SHA256 in fetch-metal.sh. The asset is 202 MB, so reading GitHub's published digest is the right way to establish it rather than downloading the archive.
tasks.notes: The task said not to download the artifact to derive a hash and to fail closed if the true value could not be established. Both were honoured: the digest came from the release's own published asset metadata, and the unset case exits non-zero with instructions instead of silently skipping verification.

tasks.title: install.sh interpolates the project path into `bash -c`, so an apostrophe in the path is command injection
tasks.discovered_by: Phase B, L3/L4 line-depth pass over tools/ and web/
tasks.evidence_before: `bash -c "cd '$ROOT' && swift run -c release chatbots-cli --check"` pastes the project path inside single quotes inside a double-quoted command string. A path containing an apostrophe breaks the quoting: the transport and model checks fail with a shell syntax error, and a crafted directory name such as `...'; cmd; echo '` is command injection at install time. The launcher written to ~/Applications has the same flaw inside its single-quoted osascript string.
tasks.fix_summary: The project path is no longer interpolated into a shell command string. A `run_in_root` helper takes the directory as its first argument and the command as the remaining words, running `( cd "$dir" || exit 1; exec "$@" )`, so an apostrophe or a semicolon in the checkout's name is just a character in a path. The generated launcher writes its paths with `printf 'ROOT=%q\n'` and passes the installer path to `osascript` as an argv item rather than pasting it into the AppleScript source, so a name containing a quote, backtick or `$` cannot break the launcher or inject into it.

tasks.title: SSE connections are never reaped, so streams and connections grow for the life of the process

tasks.evidence_before: The streamer path sends the SSE head and opening events and returns without re-arming receive(), so finish()/markClosed() - the only pruning path - can never run for that connection and isOpen stays true, so `removeAll { !$0.isOpen }` never prunes. tasks.fix_summary: A streaming connection is now watched after the response is sent. The streamer path used to send the SSE head and the opening events and then return, which meant `finish` - the only code that prunes - could never run for that connection: `isOpen` stayed true, `removeAll { !$isOpen }` never removed anything, and every page reload or dropped client left an EventStream and an NWConnection retained for the life of the process while the server kept broadcasting to a dead socket. A new `awaitClose(on:)` observes the closure instead: it re-arms `receive` while the client is idle, treats completion or an error as the end, and does not re-arm once `finish` has cancelled the connection - so a keep-alive byte from a silent client does not end a live stream, and a client that has gone is reaped.

tasks.title: CORS is `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` and every preflight is answered, so any website the user visits can read every kept conversation and drive the engine
tasks.discovered_by: closing the one declared Phase B coverage gap (web/style.css) and following the missing browser-facing defences it exposed
tasks.evidence_before: `HTTPResponse.serialised` appends `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`, `Access-Control-Allow-Headers: Content-Type` and `Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET, POST, OPTIONS` to EVERY response, including the API's. `APIServer.handle` begins `if request.method == "OPTIONS" { return HTTPResponse(status: 204) }`, which answers every cross-origin preflight with those same wide-open headers. So a page served from any origin can `fetch('http://localhost:7788/api/conversations')` and READ the reply - every kept conversation, the full transcript, the roster - and can POST to /api/conversations/new, /api/roster, /api/moderator, /api/seat and /api/attachments, because the preflight that would otherwise block a JSON write succeeds. The comment above the header says it is there because 'a browser reload during development sometimes hits the port directly', which is how a development convenience became a universal grant.
tasks.notes: Nuance, stated because it changes the practical severity: Chrome is rolling out Private Network Access, which requires a preflight carrying `Access-Control-Request-Private-Network` and a matching `Access-Control-Allow-Private-Network` response header. That header is not sent, so a current Chrome may block a public-to-localhost request. Safari and Firefox do not implement PNA, so the attack works there today, and PNA is not a defence to rely on - it is a browser rollout that does not cover the installed base. Graded S1 rather than S0 for that reason, and because A29 (arbitrary file write) is being fixed in the same pass: before A29's fix this same path was a remote file-write primitive from any web page, which would have been S0. This is independent of A01: A01 is about the LAN, this needs no network position at all, only that the user visits a hostile page while ChatBots is running.

tasks.title: No CSP, no X-Frame-Options or frame-ancestors, no X-Content-Type-Options, no Referrer-Policy
tasks.discovered_by: closing the one declared Phase B coverage gap (web/style.css) and following the missing browser-facing defences it exposed
tasks.evidence_before: `HTTPResponse.serialised` writes only Content-Type, Content-Length, Cache-Control, the wide-open CORS triple and Connection; there is no Content-Security-Policy, no X-Frame-Options or CSP frame-ancestors, no X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff and no Referrer-Policy, in the server or in Caddyfile. The interface can therefore be framed by any page the user visits, and A20's stored XSS had no CSP behind it to make it harder. The page renders model output, document text and share pages, which is exactly the content a CSP would bound. `web/style.css` itself is clean - it contains no url(), @import, expression(), javascript: or behavior() - so this is about the response headers rather than the stylesheet.
tasks.notes: Recorded while closing the one coverage gap the line-depth wave declared: the tools/web pass had grepped style.css rather than reading it. Reading it (917 lines) found nothing, so the gap is closed and this is what it exposed next door.

tasks.title: The shipped app redistributes ~14 third-party libraries with no licence notices or attribution
tasks.discovered_by: go-live readiness check on dependency licensing, run while the fix lanes were busy
tasks.evidence_before: `Package.swift` declares mlx-swift-lm, swift-huggingface, swift-transformers and Pummelchen/WebTransport; the resolved graph adds swift-argument-parser, swift-asn1, swift-collections, swift-crypto, swift-jinja, swift-numerics, swift-syntax, yyjson and EventSource, and mlx-swift's Cmlx bundles fmt, json, metal-cpp, mlx and mlx-c as C/C++ sources compiled into the binary. Licences are MIT (mlx-swift-lm, mlx-swift, WebTransport, yyjson, EventSource, fmt, json, mlx, mlx-c) and Apache-2.0 (swift-transformers, swift-huggingface, swift-crypto, swift-collections, swift-numerics, swift-syntax, swift-asn1, swift-argument-parser). All permissive, so there is no copyleft problem: the defect is attribution. The repository contains only its own LICENSE, there is no third-party notices file, and `grep -niE 'licen|notice|third.?party' tools/make-app.sh` returns nothing, so the assembled .app copies no licence text into the bundle. MIT requires the copyright and permission notice to accompany all copies or substantial portions, and Apache-2.0 requires the licence text and any NOTICE file to be retained.
tasks.notes: Cheap and mechanical to fix, and it is a release blocker for a public release rather than a security issue: generate a THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES file from the resolved dependency graph (Package.resolved pins exact revisions, so it is deterministic), commit it, include it as a package resource so it lands in the bundle, and copy it into the .app's Resources in make-app.sh alongside the icon. The check that keeps it true is that the generation step runs in the same CI job that already verifies generated files are in step (the `generated-files` job), so a dependency added without its notice fails the push rather than shipping.

tasks.title: `NSHumanReadableCopyright` carries a description instead of a copyright, and the bundle identifier and version are single-sourced in one script only
tasks.discovered_by: go-live readiness check on bundle metadata, run while the fix lanes were busy
tasks.evidence_before: The generated Info.plist sets `NSHumanReadableCopyright` to `Local build - two MLX models in conversation.` That key has a defined meaning - it is the copyright line macOS shows in the Finder's Get Info panel and in About boxes - and the value is a description of the app instead. It names no holder and no year, so a shipped build would display no copyright at all. Related, and recorded together because it is the same single-source problem: `CFBundleIdentifier` is `local.chatbots.twollms` (fine for a local build, wrong for distribution, and it appears only here), `CFBundleShortVersionString` is `1.0` and `CFBundleVersion` is `1`, both literals in the same heredoc, so an app version exists in exactly one place with nothing tying it to a release or a tag, and the repository's own LICENSE says `Copyright (c) 2026 Andre Borchert` - the holder A77 also needs for attribution.
tasks.notes: Small and in the same family as A77: this is publishing readiness rather than a runtime defect, and it is cheap because make-app.sh already generates the plist in one place. The fix is to put the real copyright line in the key, state where the bundle identifier and version come from (and change the identifier if a distributed build is intended), and make the version a single value rather than a literal repeated across the plist and any release notes. It should be done alongside A77 so the two distribution fixes land coherently, and the generated-files CI job is the natural place to keep them true.

tasks.title: Python bytecode is not ignored, so running any helper script or the CI byte-compile step leaves untracked noise
tasks.discovered_by: noticed while checking a lane's working tree: tools/__pycache__/ appeared untracked
tasks.evidence_before: .gitignore has no Python rules at all: `git check-ignore -v tools/__pycache__` returns nothing, and `grep -n 'pycache\|\.pyc\|python' .gitignore` matches nothing. `tools/` contains five Python helpers, and the `static-analysis` CI job that A04 added runs `python3 -m py_compile` over every one of them, which writes `__pycache__/`. So both running the tools locally and the push-time job leave untracked files in a tree the audit requires to be clean.
tasks.fix_summary: Added `__pycache__/` and `*.py[cod]` to .gitignore, with a comment saying why: a tree that is dirty for the wrong reason is one nobody reads, and this audit's own integrity checks (a clean tree in the Phase E script, verify-done-commits) depend on `git status` meaning something.
tasks.evidence_after: git check-ignore -v tools/__pycache__ => matches the new rule; the stray directory was removed; git status --short reports no untracked Python artefacts.
tasks.notes: S3 hygiene rather than a defect in behaviour, recorded because it was found the way the audit wants findings found - by looking at an actual working tree rather than at a document. It also matters slightly more than usual here: the new CI job byte-compiles every helper, so the noise would appear on every push.
